name: DSL-JSON (Java, HotSpot) vs nlohmann/json, json-c and Boost.PropertyTree in kostya/benchmarks JSON
baseline: nlohmann/json (C++), json-c (C) and Boost.PropertyTree (C++) as built by kostya/benchmarks; DSL-JSON does NOT beat RapidJSON, Boost.JSON, simdjson, yyjson, gason or DAW JSON Link in the same table
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-object JSON file (generate_json.rb: x, y, z doubles plus name and opts fields, pretty-printed) and compute the mean of x, y and z; the README reports median time of the benchmark execution (data loading and code self-testing are not measured).
claimed_speedup: Time in seconds (lower is better), from the kostya/benchmarks README Json table: Java (DSL-JSON) 0.571; C++/clang++ (Nlohmann) 1.182; C++/g++ (Nlohmann) 1.266; C++/clang++ (json-c) 1.185; C++/g++ (json-c) 1.187; C++/clang++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.589; C++/g++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.907. That is about 2.1-2.2x faster than Nlohmann (derived from page data). In the same table it is slower than C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154, C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374, C++/clang++ (simdjson DOM) 0.103, C/gcc (yyjson) 0.131 and C++/g++ (gason) 0.127.
compiler_and_flags: C++ built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), both with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk); nlohmann/json is cloned from its git repository and used as the single header. Managed side per the README environment table and Makefiles, Java side: DSL-JSON 2.0.2 (json/json-java/Maven.list) compiled with javac -proc:full so the @CompiledJson annotation processor generates the converter; README environment table lists Java 24.0.2 while common/commands.mk passes javac --release 26 (inconsistency in the source); HotSpot default JIT, no special JVM flags found.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G (README Environment section; Docker on Debian forky/sid); README results marked UPDATE: 2026-07-19
tradeoffs: Fast path needs compile-time databinding (annotation processor generates converters for @CompiledJson classes); the reflection variant is described as only comparable to Jackson. JVM warm-up and heap are part of the cost: the table shows 277.81 MiB base + 163.69 MiB peak increase for Java versus 113.33 + 447.88 MiB for g++ nlohmann and 113.21 + 123.44 MiB for g++ RapidJSON.
caveats: Beats only the slow C/C++ JSON libraries; the fast ones (simdjson, yyjson, gason, DAW JSON Link, RapidJSON, Boost.JSON) are about 1.5-9.5x faster than it in the same table (derived from page data), so this is not a case of Java beating the C/C++ incumbent for fast JSON. Work is not identical: the Java test deserialises straight into a generated Root/Coordinate class with JsonReader.DoublePrecision.LOW (reduced number-parsing accuracy; the README notes the same kind of inaccuracy for default RapidJSON, DAW JSON Link, gason), while the nlohmann test builds a full DOM and calls get<double>. The README says data loading and code self-testing are not measured and that JIT warm-up is not separated out; implementations are meant to be 'written as the average software developer would write them'. The DSL-JSON README itself cites this benchmark ('Kostya JSON - fastest performing Java JSON library') and makes no C++ comparison. Numbers were read from a raw README fetch; repo pages were opened on github.com for license, stars and commit date. The DSL-JSON README explanation of why it is fast is the library author's own.
found_via: Blogs / talks slice. WebSearch (github.com, 'benchmark repo C# .NET OR Java OR Julia OR LuaJIT OR SBCL outperforms C++ clang -O3 ...') did not name it; found by parsing every JIT-language row of the kostya/benchmarks README Json, Base64, Matmul and Primes tables against the best C/C++ rows. Only the Json table has managed-runtime rows ahead of any C/C++ library.
why_faster: From the DSL-JSON README FAQ: almost zero allocations, works on byte level, better algorithms for byte[] to type conversion, minimized unexpected branching, and compile-time databinding (generated converters) instead of reflection.

name: JSON3.jl (Julia) vs nlohmann/json, json-c and Boost.PropertyTree in kostya/benchmarks JSON
baseline: nlohmann/json (C++), json-c (C) and Boost.PropertyTree (C++) as built by kostya/benchmarks; JSON3 does NOT beat RapidJSON, Boost.JSON, simdjson, yyjson, gason or DAW JSON Link in the same table
workload: Parse a generated 524,288-object JSON file (generate_json.rb) and compute the mean of x, y and z using JSON3.read and iteration over jobj['coordinates'] (json/test.jl).
claimed_speedup: Time in seconds (lower is better), kostya/benchmarks README Json table: Julia (JSON3) 0.700; C++/clang++ (Nlohmann) 1.182; C++/g++ (Nlohmann) 1.266; C++/clang++ (json-c) 1.185; C++/g++ (json-c) 1.187; C++/clang++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.589; C++/g++ (Boost.PropertyTree) 2.907. About 1.7-1.8x faster than Nlohmann (derived from page data). Slower than C++/g++ (RapidJSON) 0.154, C++/g++ (Boost.JSON) 0.374 and Java (DSL-JSON) 0.571.
compiler_and_flags: C++ built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), both with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk); nlohmann/json is cloned from its git repository and used as the single header. Managed side per the README environment table and Makefiles, Julia v1.11.6 run as 'julia --optimize=3 --check-bounds=no' (common/commands.mk JULIA_RUN); json/test.jl installs JSON3 with Pkg.add at run time.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G (README Environment section; Docker on Debian forky/sid); README results marked UPDATE: 2026-07-19
tradeoffs: Package is deprecated in its own README ('migrate to JSON.jl v1'); the last commit only fixes compatibility with Julia 1.13. Memory in the table is 631.76 MiB base + 332.81 MiB increase, far above the C++ rows. Lazy tape-based reading.
caveats: Capped at C because the source gives no mechanism: the JSON3 README only says it is 'for speed and slick struct mapping'. Beats only the slow C/C++ libraries; the fast ones are about 1.8-11.7x faster in the same table (derived from page data). JSON3.read builds a lazy index and values are materialised on access, while the nlohmann test builds a full DOM, so the work is not the same. The README does not separate Julia JIT compile time from the measured run. Package deprecated, so listing it is mainly evidence for the JSON.jl v1 successor, which was not measured here.
found_via: Blogs / talks slice. Parsed the kostya/benchmarks README Json table for managed-runtime rows ahead of C/C++ libraries (same pass as DSL-JSON); confirmed json/test.jl uses JSON3.

name: lua-resty-core (LuaJIT FFI API for ngx_lua) vs the ngx_lua built-in Lua C API
baseline: the Lua C API implementation of the ngx.* and ngx.shared.* functions in lua-nginx-module (ngx_lua, C)
workload: Calls of the ngx_lua API functions from Lua code running under LuaJIT through the FFI-based reimplementation versus the C API implementation; no workload is specified.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. README: 'its FFI implementation is both faster, safer, and more complete than the Lua C API of the ngx_lua module.' Caveat in the same README: 'You will only observe speedup when you get a good part of your user Lua code JIT compiled.'
stars_or_usage: 855 stars, 288 forks; part of the OpenResty project
tradeoffs: Requires LuaJIT with FFI and a matching nginx build; replaces parts of the C API, so API coverage differs ('more complete' per README).
caveats: Qualitative claim only, no benchmark in the README and none found elsewhere; kept as the one tier D record because of project notability, with 855 stars it sits just under the 1k guideline. License text in the README is the two-clause BSD text (SPDX id inferred). The baseline is a module C API, not a standalone C or C++ program, and the claimed gain comes from C-API calls being opaque to the tracing JIT. No hardware, versions or flags. The openresty.org pages and mailing-list posts that may hold numbers were not reachable.
found_via: Blogs / talks slice. Fetched github.com/topics/luajit (no performance claims in the 20 repository descriptions shown), then read the README of openresty/lua-resty-core, which states the FFI-versus-C-API speed claim.
why_faster: README: the Lua C API 'will never be JIT compiled and the user Lua code is always interpreted (slowly)', while the FFI-based API calls can be JIT compiled by LuaJIT.
